6.10 Risk Management and Common Mistakes

This content was generated by AI. It may contain errors and is not investment advice.

All lessons, questions and reference answers on this site were generated by AI and have not been reviewed by a professional. Their correctness is not guaranteed. If you find an error, please report it with the link at the bottom of the page. The content is for learning only and is not investment advice.

The largest losses in household investing often come not from picking the wrong fund but from a few common mistakes: investing with borrowed money, trying to time the market, chasing returns, trading too much and concentrating too much. This lesson looks at each in turn, and at how rules written in advance can help avoid them.

Leverage

Section titled “Leverage”

Investing with borrowed money magnifies both gains and losses (financial leverage). Margin loans in a brokerage account (margin) carry an extra risk: when the share of the account’s own funds falls below the maintenance requirement, the broker demands more money or sells the holdings. This tends to happen after large market falls, turning a temporary fall into a real loss.

Another common form of leverage is the leveraged ETF, for example a fund that seeks twice the index’s daily return. It resets its leverage every day, so when held for more than a day its return is not twice the index’s return over that period (4.1 Measuring Return and Risk).

Check C1
Over a month, an index swings up and down day after day and ends the month where it started. A leveraged ETF seeking twice the index's daily return most likely ends the month:
Try a two-day example: the index rises 10% and then falls about 9.1%, back to where it was. A 2x ETF rises 20% and then falls about 18.2%; where does it end?
Leverage magnifies each day's fall just as much. In a choppy market, when magnified rises and falls are multiplied, is the result higher or lower than before?

Market timing

Section titled “Market timing”

Market timing means moving between stocks and cash based on a view of the market. It requires two correct decisions: when to sell, and when to buy back. The market’s best days and worst days often come in the same turbulent periods, and people who leave the market to avoid falls easily miss the rebounds that follow. Since the market rises in most years, the opportunity cost of holding cash is ongoing (Exercises Question 3).

Check C2
When stocks crashed in March 2020, an investor sold everything, planning to "buy back once things are clearer". The biggest problem with this plan is:
Most brokers charge very low commissions today. Which is larger, the cost of missing a rebound or the trading fee?
How much of the fall had he already suffered when he sold? When he buys back, and at what price, decides the result.

Why investors lag their own funds

Section titled “Why investors lag their own funds”

A fund’s reported return is its time-weighted return: the geometric average of period returns, as if a lump sum had been invested at the start and held. What an investor actually earns is the dollar-weighted return: the rate that makes the net present value of all cash flows zero, taking into account the timing and size of each purchase and withdrawal, that is, the internal rate of return (internal rate of return). If investors put in more after a fund has risen and take money out after it has fallen, the dollar-weighted return falls below the time-weighted return.

Morningstar’s “Mind the Gap” study (2025) found that over the 10 years to the end of 2024, US fund investors’ dollar-weighted returns averaged about 1.2 percentage points a year less than the time-weighted returns of the funds they held, about 15% of the total return; the gap was about 1.5 percentage points for sector funds, while allocation funds such as target-date funds showed almost no gap.

Check C3
In Figure 3-1, set k to 0, so the investor puts in a fixed 20 each year without chasing returns. His dollar-weighted return still differs slightly from the fund's time-weighted return. The reason is:
In the figure the investor and the fund face the same returns. Where does the difference come from?
Fixed amounts do not change with returns; is that chasing? Think about how much money is in the account in each year.

Overtrading and concentration

Section titled “Overtrading and concentration”

Frequent trading adds trading costs and, in taxable accounts, turns long-term gains into short-term gains taxed at higher rates (6.5 Accounts and Taxes (US)). Barber and Odean’s research showed that the individual investors who traded most earned the worst returns (4.8 Behavioral Finance). Overconfidence leads people to overrate their information and judgment, while the other side of their trades is often a better-informed professional.

Concentration is another common risk: putting most of one’s wealth in employer stock, one industry or a few stocks (6.6 The Household Balance Sheet and Insurance, 6.8 The Stock Research Process). A concentrated portfolio may bring very high returns, but it may also bring losses that cannot be recovered, and the idiosyncratic risk it carries earns no compensation (4.4 The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM)).

Check C4
Why is the extra risk of concentrating most of one's wealth in a few stocks usually not compensated by higher expected returns?
A few stocks need not have lower expected returns. The question is whether their extra risk is matched by extra reward.
A concentrated portfolio need not have a higher beta, and beta risk is compensated anyway. Which part is not?

Investment discipline

Section titled “Investment discipline”

Most of these mistakes happen when emotions run high: panic in a crash, excitement in a boom. The remedy is to write down rules in advance, while calm. The investment policy statement (IPS) is such a document: it states the household’s goals, horizon, risk capacity, strategic allocation (6.7 Asset Allocation), rebalancing rules, criteria for choosing funds, and the circumstances under which these may be changed (6.13 Monitoring and Review).

Beyond the IPS, a short discipline checklist can be consulted whenever one feels like trading, for example: Does the IPS call for this trade? If not, what is my reason, and how will I check it afterwards? Making saving and rebalancing automatic also reduces the number of decisions to be made.

Check C5
Once written, an investment policy statement should never be changed under any circumstances, or it loses its power to restrain.
What is the IPS based on? Would those bases change if the household had a child, changed jobs or neared retirement? Would a market crash change them?

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • Margin loans can be forcibly closed after a crash; leveraged ETFs reset leverage daily, so their long-run return is not a fixed multiple of the index’s.
  • Market timing requires being right twice; the opportunity cost of being out of the market is ongoing.
  • Investors’ dollar-weighted returns often fall below their funds’ time-weighted returns, mainly because of return chasing.
  • Frequent trading adds costs and taxes; concentration bears idiosyncratic risk that is not compensated.
  • An investment policy statement and a discipline checklist set rules while calm, to restrain emotional decisions.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1
An investor uses 50,000 dollars of his own money plus a 50,000 dollar margin loan to buy 100,000 dollars of a stock index fund. The broker's maintenance requirement is 25% (own funds must be at least 25% of the stocks' market value).
(a) At what percentage fall in price does he get a margin call?
(b) He says: "I'm a long-term investor, short-term falls don't affect me, and the loan rate is only 6%, below stocks' long-run return, so investing with borrowed money is a good deal." Evaluate this statement.
Question 2
An index rises 10% on the first day and falls 10% on the second. A leveraged ETF seeking twice the index's daily return resets its leverage daily.
(a) After two days, by what percentage have the index and the leveraged ETF changed?
(b) An investor says: "I'm bullish on stocks for the next 10 years, so I'll buy a 2x leveraged ETF and hold it for 10 years to get twice the index return." Evaluate this statement. Under what conditions might a leveraged ETF's long-run return exceed twice the index's?
Question 3
Suppose stocks rise in 70% of years, averaging +20% in up years, and fall in 30% of years, averaging −15%; cash returns 3% a year. A market timer calls each year's direction at the start: if he calls up he holds stocks, if down he holds cash; he is right with probability ppp, regardless of what the market actually does.
(a) What is the expected yearly return of always holding stocks? What is the timer's expected return as a function of ppp? How large must ppp be for timing to do no worse than always holding stocks (ignoring trading costs and taxes)?
(b) He says: "I call the direction right 60% of the time, better than a coin flip, so timing raises my returns." Evaluate this statement.
Question 4
A fund rises 50% in the first year and falls 40% in the second. An investor puts in 100 at the start of year one and, after seeing year one's performance, another 200 at the start of year two; the account balance at the end of year two is what he has.
(a) What is the fund's time-weighted yearly return over the two years? What is the investor's dollar-weighted yearly return (IRR)?
(b) He says: "The fund reports only about −5% a year, yet I lost so much; the fund's figures must be wrong." Evaluate this statement, and say how such an outcome can be avoided.
